title: Hard-Soft Acid-Base Theory Explains Photoexcited Carrier Dynamics in Porphyrin/CNT Nanohybrids: Time-Domain Atomistic Analysis.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Introduction Fossil fuels emit greenhouse gases in
the environment, causing
global warming, pollution, and other societal problems.  Solar energy provides an excellent alternative
to overcome this critical issue.  A photovoltaic
cell is required to have fast photoinduced charge transfer and delayed
electron–hole (e-h) recombination in order to convert solar
radiation into electricity efficiently. 
 , 
  The donor–acceptor
nanohybrid strategy is effective in this regard because it allows
the photogenerated charges to be separated easily at the interface. 
 − 
 
  Semiconducting single-walled carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are promising
photovoltaic materials due to strong light absorption,  large π-electron surface available for interfacial
interactions, 
 , 
  excellent charge transport properties, 
 , 
  low cost,  and outstanding electron-accepting
capacity.  In addition, CNTs show excellent
thermal and chemical stability, which prevents their photodegradation. 
 , 
  The unique combination of structural, electronic, mechanical, and
optoelectronic properties 
 − 
 
  motivates diverse CNT applications
in solar cells,  lasers,  light-emitting diodes, 
 , 
  field-effect
transistors, 
 , 
  water oxidation,  hydrogen storage, 
 , 
  sensors,  computers,  thin-film
conductors, 
 , 
  and displays.  Designing donor–acceptor CNT nanohybrids with suitable
photosensitizers attracts particular attention. The large π-conjugated
surface of CNTs allows noncovalent interaction with π-conjugated
counterparts without disturbing the π-electron network and optical
properties of the tubes. This approach has been widely applied for
building CNT-based donor–acceptor architectures utilizing porphyrins, 
 , 
  fullerenes, 
 , 
  squaraine,  π-extended tetrathiafulvalene, 
 , 
  pyrene,  perylene diimide, 
 , 
  and polymers.  Zinc porphyrins (ZnPs)
are appealing candidates for photovoltaic applications due to their
outstanding performance as light-harvesting antennas, 
 , 
  light-emitting diodes,  photosensitizers,  and photocatalysts.  The delocalized π-electrons of ZnP facilitate π–π
stacking with CNTs, making van der Waals ZnP/CNT nanocomposites promising
for photoconversion. 
 , , , 
 
 The photoinduced excited-state dynamics
of ZnP/CNT composites were
studied in the past. For example, D’Souza et al. demonstrated
photoinduced electron transfer (ET) in donor–acceptor self-assembled
ZnP/CNT nanohybrids by transient absorption studies. 
 , 
  Ito et al. investigated photoexcited carrier relaxation in noncovalent
porphyrin/DNA-wrapped CNT hybrids.  They
observed ultrafast charge transfer and slow recombination across the
interface in a nanosecond time regime. Zinc-based nanohybrids generate
photocurrents stronger than those of metal-free composites. Pal et
al. investigated the carrier dynamics of noncovalent porphyrin/CNT
nanohybrids by atomistic time-domain simulation.  They showed ultrafast charge separation and delayed recombination
and reported that porphyrin stereochemistry influences the dynamics.
Studies of acidity-dependent carrier dynamics are rare. Zhou et al.
investigated the pH-dependent exciton lifetime of graphitic carbon
nitride quantum dots.  The dependence
of carrier recombination in ligated perovskite nanocrystals on surface
ligand acidity was reported by Diau et al.  Acidity-dependent carrier relaxation dynamics in porphyrin/CNT hybrids
are still unexplored, motivating us to investigate the carrier dynamics
of the recently synthesized ZnP/CNT hybrids. 
 In this work, we demonstrate how the charge separation and
recombination
dynamics in noncovalent ZnP/CNT nanohybrids can be controlled by a
rational choice of a substituent and explain this effect by a detailed
analysis of the time-domain atomistic simulation and general chemical
principles. Photoexcitation of a ZnP results in a subpicosecond ET
to the CNT, in agreement with the experiment.  Replacement of the electron-withdrawing cyano (CN) group at the
ZnP β-pyrrolic position with a hydrogen (H) atom accelerates
the ET, and substitution of CN by the electron-donating tertiary ( t Bu) group makes the ET even faster. The established ET trend
is rationalized at the atomistic level by changes in the electronic
structure, nonadiabatic (NA) coupling, quantum coherence, and participation
of particular vibrational modes. Referring to the general chemical
principles, the least acidic  t Bu-ZnP exhibits favorable
soft–soft acid–base interaction with the soft base CNT,
enhancing the overlap of the donor and acceptor orbitals and strengthening
the NA coupling between the relevant adiabatic states. The longer-lived
quantum coherence and involvement of a broader range of vibrational
motions assist with the fast ET in the  t Bu-ZnP/CNT hybrid.
The simulations demonstrate that the ET time scales correlate strongly
with p K 
 a  of the β-pyrrolic acid.
The larger the p K 
 a , the faster the through-space
ET. The electron-hole (e-h) recombination is the fastest across the
CN-ZnP/CNT heterointerface and occurs on a hundred picosecond time
scale, also in agreement with the experiment.  The lifetime of the charge-separated state extends beyond a nanosecond
upon substitution of CN with H and  t Bu. The charge recombination
is the slowest in the  t Bu-ZnP/CNT hybrid due to weak NA
coupling, fast quantum coherence loss, and involvement of only low-frequency
vibrational modes. The observed trend of the charge recombination
dynamics is also rationalized by the hard–soft acid–base
(HSAB) principle. The hard–soft interaction in the CN-ZnP/CNT
hybrid creates a small valence band (VB) offset that enhances mixing
of the highest occupied orbitals of the ZnP and the CNT, and creates
a stronger NA coupling. The energy offset is comparable with the thermal
energy at 300 K, and thus, CN-ZnP/CNT exhibits a quasi-type-II energy
alignment. In comparison, the matching soft–soft interaction
in  t Bu-ZnP/CNT enlarges the VB energy offset, reducing
the orbital mixing and the NA coupling and prolonging the carrier
recombination. The state-of-the-art simulation underscores that fast
charge transfer and delayed e-h recombination are achieved by tuning
the p K 
 a  of the ZnP unit. The higher the
p K 
 a  value, the slower the charge recombination.
By establishing p K 
 a  as a marker for predicting
the ET and e-h recombination times, we demonstrate a key relationship
between apparently distinct properties and molecular structure. The
atomistic investigation provides detailed information on the mechanism
of the excited-state dynamics of charge carriers in an important class
of modern nanomaterials, providing essential insights for the development
of future photovoltaic and optoelectronic devices.

sections.heading: Simulation Details
sections.text:
Simulation Details The simulation box of the investigated
system contains one unit
cell of (6,5) CNT and a ZnP molecule noncovalently self-assembled
on the surface of the tube. The CNT is periodic in the  z -direction, with a cell length of 41 Å. A vacuum of 41 Å
in length is included along the  x - and  y -directions to avoid spurious interactions between the periodic images
of the simulation cell. The diameter of the (6,5) CNT is 7.57 Å.
The total numbers of atoms in the unit cells are 477, 476, and 488
for CN-ZnP/CNT, H-ZnP/CNT, and  t Bu-ZnP/CNT respectively.
The photoinduced ET and e-h recombination dynamics of the ZnP/CNT
nanohybrids are investigated by nonadiabatic molecular dynamics (NAMD)
combined with the self-consistent charge density functional tight
binding (SCC-DFTB) theory.  SCC-DFTB can
treat large systems (more than a thousand atoms) with reasonable accuracy
and low computational cost. In NAMD, the electronic degrees of freedom
are treated quantum-mechanically, while atomic motions are treated
classically by solving Newton’s equation, or semiclassically.
The electronic subsystem exerts a quantum force that directs the dynamics
of the atoms, and the atomic subsystem generates a classical external
field that governs the evolution of the electronic subsystem. The
classical path approximation (CPA) is applied within NAMD. 
 , 
  The CPA operates if atomic motions do not exhibit strong dependence
on the electronic state, which is the case in the present systems
that do not exhibit isomerization, deformation, and fragmentation
after electronic excitation. The fewest switches surface hopping (FSSH)
approach 
 , 
  is applied to simulate the ET dynamics.
To account for the decoherence effect in the NAMD simulation, decoherence-induced
surface hopping (DISH) 
 , 
  is used to simulate the charge
recombination. The details of the theoretical methodology can be found
in the  Supporting Information. 
 All
quantum mechanical calculations involved in the electronic
structure, geometry optimization, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations
are performed by SCC-DFTB  implemented
in the DFTB+ package.  The DFTB mio parameter
data set  is utilized for C, H, N, and
O. For Zn, the parameter data set was generated by Sarkar et al.  is used. It is compatible with the mio data
set and has been tested for a large variety of systems. 
 , , − 
 
 
 
 
 
  The Lennard-Jones dispersion potentials are used to characterize
the noncovalent interactions.  After the
geometry optimization, the ZnP/CNT nanohybrids are heated to room
temperature for 5 ps by applying velocity rescaling.  Then, 3 ps MD trajectories are generated using the Verlet
algorithm with a 1 fs time-step.  The
trajectories are used to calculate the time-dependent Kohn–Sham
(KS) orbital energies and NA coupling matrix elements between the
energy eigenstates. The NA coupling calculations are performed to
generate a time-dependent Hamiltonian for the NAMD simulation. The
FSSH and DISH algorithms are implemented in the PYthon eXtension for
Ab Initio Dynamics (PYXAID) code. 
 , 
  To generate
the initial conditions for NAMD, we used the first 1000 geometries
of the 3 ps adiabatic trajectories and started the NAMD simulations
from each of these geometries. We promoted an electron from ZnP HOMO
to L+4 for CN-ZnP/CNT, whereas for H-ZnP/CNT and tBu-ZnP/CNT, an electron
was excited from ZnP HOMO to L+8 at the initial time. For each initial
geometry, we sampled 1000 stochastic realizations of the surface hopping
procedures. NAMD combined with SCC-DFTB can efficiently and accurately
reproduce the photoinduced carrier relaxation time scales in a broad
range of systems, including CNTs 
 , 
  and its hybrids, 
 , , 
  cadmium chalcogenide nanoplatelets, 
 − 
 
  quantum dots,  and macromolecular porphyrin
nanorings.

enhancing the overlap of the donor and acceptor orbitals and strengthening
the NA coupling between the relevant adiabatic states. The longer-lived
quantum coherence and involvement of a broader range of vibrational
motions assist with the fast ET in the  t Bu-ZnP/CNT hybrid.
The simulations demonstrate that the ET time scales correlate strongly
with p K 
 a  of the β-pyrrolic acid.
The larger the p K 
 a , the faster the through-space
ET. The electron-hole (e-h) recombination is the fastest across the
CN-ZnP/CNT heterointerface and occurs on a hundred picosecond time
scale, also in agreement with the experiment.  The lifetime of the charge-separated state extends beyond a nanosecond
upon substitution of CN with H and  t Bu. The charge recombination
is the slowest in the  t Bu-ZnP/CNT hybrid due to weak NA
coupling, fast quantum coherence loss, and involvement of only low-frequency
vibrational modes. The observed trend of the charge recombination
dynamics is also rationalized by the hard–soft acid–base
(HSAB) principle. The hard–soft interaction in the CN-ZnP/CNT
hybrid creates a small valence band (VB) offset that enhances mixing
of the highest occupied orbitals of the ZnP and the CNT, and creates
a stronger NA coupling. The energy offset is comparable with the thermal
energy at 300 K, and thus, CN-ZnP/CNT exhibits a quasi-type-II energy
alignment. In comparison, the matching soft–soft interaction
in  t Bu-ZnP/CNT enlarges the VB energy offset, reducing
the orbital mixing and the NA coupling and prolonging the carrier
recombination. The state-of-the-art simulation underscores that fast
charge transfer and delayed e-h recombination are achieved by tuning
the p K 
 a  of the ZnP unit. The higher the
p K 
 a  value, the slower the charge recombination.
By establishing p K 
 a  as a marker for predicting
the ET and e-h recombination times, we demonstrate a key relationship
between apparently distinct properties and molecular structure. The
atomistic investigation provides detailed information on the mechanism
of the excited-state dynamics of charge carriers in an important class
of modern nanomaterials, providing essential insights for the development
of future photovoltaic and optoelectronic devices.

Simulation Details The simulation box of the investigated
system contains one unit
cell of (6,5) CNT and a ZnP molecule noncovalently self-assembled
on the surface of the tube. The CNT is periodic in the  z -direction, with a cell length of 41 Å. A vacuum of 41 Å
in length is included along the  x - and  y -directions to avoid spurious interactions between the periodic images
of the simulation cell. The diameter of the (6,5) CNT is 7.57 Å.
The total numbers of atoms in the unit cells are 477, 476, and 488
for CN-ZnP/CNT, H-ZnP/CNT, and  t Bu-ZnP/CNT respectively.
The photoinduced ET and e-h recombination dynamics of the ZnP/CNT
nanohybrids are investigated by nonadiabatic molecular dynamics (NAMD)
combined with the self-consistent charge density functional tight
binding (SCC-DFTB) theory.  SCC-DFTB can
treat large systems (more than a thousand atoms) with reasonable accuracy
and low computational cost. In NAMD, the electronic degrees of freedom
are treated quantum-mechanically, while atomic motions are treated
classically by solving Newton’s equation, or semiclassically.
The electronic subsystem exerts a quantum force that directs the dynamics
of the atoms, and the atomic subsystem generates a classical external
field that governs the evolution of the electronic subsystem. The
classical path approximation (CPA) is applied within NAMD. 
 , 
  The CPA operates if atomic motions do not exhibit strong dependence
on the electronic state, which is the case in the present systems
that do not exhibit isomerization, deformation, and fragmentation
after electronic excitation. The fewest switches surface hopping (FSSH)
approach 
 , 
  is applied to simulate the ET dynamics.
To account for the decoherence effect in the NAMD simulation, decoherence-induced
surface hopping (DISH) 
 , 
  is used to simulate the charge
recombination. The details of the theoretical methodology can be found
in the  Supporting Information.

Charge Carrier Dynamics Photoexcitation of a ZnP leads
to ET from the ZnP LUMO to the CNT CBM across the ZnP/CNT interface.
The ET process occurs by transfer of the population of the initial
state localized on ZnP to the manifold of states in the CNT conduction
band, below in energy than the initial state. Once the population
leaves the initial state, the electron becomes localized on the CNT.
Therefore, the decay of the population of the initial state localized
on the ZnP is a direct measure of the ET process. Once the photoexcited
electron relaxes to the bottom of the CNT conduction band, charge
recombination occurs by transition across the system’s energy
gap, populating the ground electronic state. Therefore, the population
of the ground electronic state is the direct measure of charge recombination. We perform NAMD simulations of this process and obtain the ET time
scales by fitting the population decay data with a linear combination
of the exponential and Gaussian functions:

Gaussian or cosine function, as exemplified by the initial stage of
the Rabi oscillation. The first derivative of the population of the
initial state at time zero is zero. In particular, this gives rise
to the quantum Zeno effect.

over time, it becomes irreversible due to the involvement of many
states and coupling to a vibrational bath. The Rabi oscillation turns
into exponential decay. We use the combination of the Gaussian and
exponential functions to reflect both the early Gaussian and later

Conclusion We applied the DFTB and NAMD approaches
to study the photoinduced
dynamics of charge carriers at the ZnP/CNT van der Waals heterojunctions.
Upon ZnP photoexcitation, ultrafast ET takes place from the ZnP to
the CNT on a subpicosecond time scale. The CN-ZnP/CNT hybrid shows
the slowest ET. Substitution of CN by H accelerates the ET. The fastest
ET occurs when CN is replaced by  t Bu, accelerating the
process 3-fold. The trend is rationalized by the HSAB interaction
concept. In particular, the matching soft–soft acid–base
interaction in  t Bu-ZnP/CNT enhances the overlap of the
donor and acceptor orbitals and strengthens the NA coupling responsible
for the ET. Longer quantum coherence and coupling to a broader range
of vibrational motions accelerate the ET in  t Bu-ZnP/CNT
further. The simulations demonstrate that the ET time scales correlate
strongly with the p K 
 a  of the β-pyrrolic
acid of ZnP: the higher the p K 
 a , the faster
the ET. The charge-separated state decays to the ground state
through nonradiative
e-h recombination within 300 ps in the CN-ZnP/CNT hybrid. The carrier
lifetime increases to over a nanosecond by a factor of 4 when CN is
substituted by H and by a factor of 6 when CN is substituted by  t Bu. The carrier lifetime is prolonged by weaker NA coupling,
faster quantum decoherence, and coupling to lower frequency vibrational
modes. The trend in the charge recombination dynamics is also rationalized
by the HSAB principle. The interaction is hard–soft for CN-ZnP/CNT,
creating a small VB offset. The soft–soft matching interaction
in  t Bu-ZnP/CNT creates the largest VB offset, thereby reducing
orbital mixing at the VB edge and the overlap of the electron and
hole wave functions. A poor overlap weakens the NA coupling and extends
the lifetime of the charge-separated state in  t Bu-ZnP/CNT.
We have established ZnP β-pyrrolic p K 
 a  as a marker for predicting the carrier lifetime: The higher the
p K 
 a , the slower the charge recombination. The reported state-of-the-art simulation underscores the following
observations. First, the theoretical approach adopted in this work
provides a good description of the experimental observations, supporting
the methodology. Second, the ZnP/CNT van der Waals heterojunction
can efficiently dissociate photogenerated excitons, leading to ultrafast
ET and a long-lived charge-separated state. Third, the fast charge
transfer and delayed recombination are achieved by tuning the acidity
of the photoactive donor subsystem. Fourth, the excited-state carrier
relaxation is sensitive to the β-pyrrolic substituent in the
photoactive ZnP electron donor. Fifth, modifications to the β-pyrrolic
ligand with simple groups such as CN,  t Bu, and even the
smallest H significantly modulate the quantum transition rates. Sixth,
the electron-withdrawing CN group delays the ET while accelerating
the charge recombination. In turn, the electron-donating  t Bu group accelerates the ET while minimizing the charge recombination.
Seventh, p K 
 a  of the ZnP β-pyrrolic
acid can be regarded as a predictive tool to obtain information on
the lifetime of the photogenerated carriers. Eighth, a chemist can
engineer the electronic structure and carrier relaxation times in
ZnP/CNT and related hybrids by rationally creating photoactive components
with large p K 
 a  to improve the photoconversion.
Ninth, the HSAB principle plays a significant role in the carrier
dynamics of the ZnP/CNT composite. The soft–soft interaction
accelerates ET and reduces e-h recombination compared to the hard–soft
interaction. The reported atomistic investigation provides a detailed
mechanism of carrier relaxation dynamics at the CNT-based van der
Waals heterojunctions for the development of future photovoltaic and
optoelectronic applications.
